title: You Don’t Work for Me
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The argument here is that the phrase 'works for me' quietly manufactures passivity, and that leaders should push the correction downward: you work with me, not for me. The author describes a 'boss effect' in which people who believe they work for a leader wait for instructions, seek approval before deciding, filter what they say, and volunteer ideas only on request — and keep doing so even when the leader is absent. Deference is treated as natural rather than pathological, rooted in human status-sensitivity and reinforced by organizational hierarchy, which is precisely why leaders must actively fight it. The prescribed remedy is linguistic and specific: call yourself the team leader rather than the boss, swap 'you' for 'we,' and retire the possessive 'my team, my people, my results' in favor of 'our.' The claimed payoff is that leaders who do not see people as working for them defer more readily to others' expertise and get more candid dissent. The piece ends with an inversion: experienced leaders privately know they work harder for any given team member than that member works for them.
points: The 'boss effect' is described with concrete behavioral symptoms — waiting for instructions, seeking approval, self-filtering, withholding ideas — which makes it diagnosable rather than abstract.
Deference is framed as natural human status-sensitivity amplified by hierarchy, so the author's point is that it must be actively resisted, not merely disclaimed.
The intervention is at the level of vocabulary: team leader instead of boss, 'we' instead of 'you,' 'our results' instead of 'my results.'
The author connects anti-deference language to decision quality — leaders who reject the 'works for me' frame defer more to subject-matter expertise and hear more candid opinion.
The closing inversion is the piece's most quotable move: good leaders privately recognize they work harder for each team member than that member works for them.
quotes: You work with me, not for me. Even leaders who excel at holding others accountable understand the importance of this distinction in how team members engage.

When people have it in their mind that they work for a leader, they operate differently. They wait for instructions, seek approval to make decisions, edit or filter what they say, and offer new ideas only when asked. This so-called boss effect creates a team of followers who wait to be directed anytime the leader is present, and often when they’re not.
As social animals, respecting authority and status is part of being human. The natural hierarchy of organizations and teams plays to this deference.

The first line of defense against unnecessary deference is the language leaders use to describe the relationship they most desire with team members. Inclusive leaders refer to themselves as the team leader, never the boss.

Leaders who don’t think of team members as working for them are much more likely to defer to the judgment and subject matter expertise of others. They encourage the healthy exchange of ideas and viewpoints critical to quality decision-making. They remind themselves they are never the smartest person in the room because that undermines the willingness of others to contribute their candid opinions.

This all starts with the projection of who really works for whom. Objectively speaking, good leaders with experience secretly recognize that they work much harder for any given team member than that team member works for them. Why not admit it and act and speak accordingly?
